questions.q: Walking the classification checklist for 'sorting a list of n numbers,' what is the correct classification and why?
options: P -- a classical algorithm like merge sort solves it directly in O(n log n), polynomial time, so the checklist stops at question 1
In BQP only, with no known classical solution
No known quantum advantage, but also unsolved classically
NP-complete -- because checking a sorted list takes some time to verify
questions.explain: Sorting is solvable directly in polynomial time (O(n log n)), which places it in P. Once a problem is confirmed to be in P, there's no need to analyze certificates or quantum speedups -- P is the most specific and complete answer.

questions.q: For the Traveling Salesman decision problem ('is there a route visiting all cities with total length <= k?'), what does the lab conclude about any quantum advantage?
options: It is solvable in classical polynomial time, so no quantum algorithm is needed

No known exponential quantum advantage exists -- the only generally applicable quantum technique (Grover's algorithm) gives at most a quadratic speedup on the underlying brute-force search, and the search space remains exponential
It has been proven that no quantum computer could ever help with this problem in any way
Shor's algorithm solves it in polynomial time on a quantum computer
questions.explain: TSP-decision is NP-complete. The best general quantum tool for brute-force search over NP-complete problem spaces is Grover's algorithm, which only offers a quadratic speedup -- leaving the problem exponential overall, with no known exponential quantum speedup the way Shor's algorithm provides for factoring.

questions.q: For factoring a 2048-bit RSA modulus, what is the correct, carefully-stated classification from the lab?
options: It is in BQP via Shor's algorithm (polynomial time on a quantum computer), it is not known to be in classical P, and the quantum speedup relative to the best known classical algorithm (GNFS) is exponential
It has been proven to be NP-complete and unsolvable by any computer
It has no known quantum algorithm at all
It is in P classically, making RSA fundamentally insecure even without quantum computers
questions.explain: Shor's algorithm factors in time polynomial in the bit-length, putting factoring in BQP. No efficient classical algorithm is known (the best is the sub-exponential General Number Field Sieve), so factoring is not known to be in classical P -- that gap is exactly the exponential speedup Shor's algorithm represents.

questions.q: For searching an unstructured database of N = 1,000,000,000 records for one matching entry, roughly how many oracle queries does Grover's algorithm need, using floor((pi/4) * sqrt(N)), compared to the classical worst case?
options: About 500,000,000 quantum queries, half the classical worst case
About 24,836 quantum queries, versus up to 1,000,000,000 classical queries in the worst case
About 1,000,000,000 quantum queries, identical to the classical worst case
Exactly 1 quantum query regardless of database size
questions.explain: sqrt(1,000,000,000) is about 31,622.8, and floor((pi/4) * 31,622.8) = 24,836. That's a genuine quadratic speedup over the classical worst case of up to a billion checks -- but notably not an exponential one.

questions.q: What is Mistake 2 that the lab specifically warns against when classifying quantum speedups?
options: Assuming every problem in NP is automatically unsolvable by any computer
Assuming that any problem with a known quantum algorithm must have an exponential speedup, when most known quantum speedups (including Grover's) are only quadratic
Assuming that P and NP are the same class of problems
Assuming that classical computers can never verify a certificate in polynomial time
questions.explain: The lab stresses that 'a quantum algorithm exists' and 'exponential speedup' are not the same claim. Only problems with specific exploitable structure (like Shor's hidden periodicity) get exponential speedups; the generically applicable Grover's algorithm only ever delivers a quadratic one.
